props.title: The Underneath
props.initialSlug: Bank heist thriller spins web of betrayal & deceit

sections.content: Steven Soderbergh's neo-noir **The Underneath** (1995) reimagines the classic film noir Criss Cross (1949) with a distinctly 90s psychological edge. Like his breakthrough **Sex, Lies and Videotape** (1989), Soderbergh experiments with nonlinear storytelling and saturated color schemes to heighten the psychological tension. Peter Gallagher's Michael Chambers echoes Burt Lancaster's doomed protagonist, but with added layers of post-modern self-awareness that became Soderbergh's trademark before his mainstream breakthrough with **Out of Sight** (1998).

sections.content: The film's complex heist plot serves as a framework for Soderbergh to explore themes of homecoming and redemption through a distinctly noir lens. His innovative use of color-coding different timelines - cool blues for the present, warm ambers for flashbacks - influenced later neo-noirs like **Memento** (2000) and **Brick** (2005). The armored car robbery sequence demonstrates Soderbergh's early mastery of tension, rivaling similar scenes in **Heat** (1995) and **Point Break** (1991).

While not as commercially successful as later Soderbergh crime films like **Ocean's Eleven** (2001), **The Underneath** showcases his ability to blend arthouse sensibilities with genre conventions. The film's exploration of family dynamics and betrayal echoes classic noirs like **Double Indemnity** (1944) while anticipating the psychological complexity of modern crime dramas like **Drive** (2011) and **Nightcrawler** (2014). movies.title: The Last Seduction
movies.slug: Linda Fiorentino delivers a powerhouse performance as a femme fatale who manipulates men in this acclaimed neo-noir

sections.content: **The Underneath** arrived during a fertile period for neo-noir, alongside films like **One False Move** (1992) and The Last Seduction (1994). These films updated noir traditions with contemporary themes and visual styles while maintaining the genre's core focus on moral ambiguity and fatalistic outcomes. Soderbergh's film particularly excels in its use of location, turning Austin, Texas into a character itself, much like how **Body Heat** (1981) used Florida's humid atmosphere to enhance its noir elements.
